newsitem.title: CANADA: Abacan CEO says investors overreacted.
newsitem.headline: Abacan CEO says investors overreacted.

text.p: The chief executive of Abacan Resource Corp, whose stock was pummelled on Monday after news of lower-than-expected production and cash flow and a postponed debt financing, said investors overreacted and the company's operations remained intact.
"The fundamentals are still there. Nothing's changed," Abacan Chief Executive Wade Cherwayko said in a telephone interview.
"We're still producing oil and the long-term potential's still there with the portfolio we've put together," he said.

Abacan lost more than 60 percent of its market value on Monday after the company said it would show lower-than-projected cash flow because of reduced average production, lower world oil prices and higher-than-expected project startup costs.
The company, which is developing oil and gas prospects off the coast of West Africa, also said it would postpone a US$160 million junk bond offering in light of the reduced expectations.

Abacan shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange fell 5.03 to 3.07 on volume of more than 11.5 million shares. The company's Nasdaq-listed shares plummeted 3-9/16 to close at 2-1/4 with nearly 22.2 million shares changing hands.
The Calgary-based company's stock topped the most-active lists of both markets.

Abacan's oil production, primarily from its Ngo field in Nigeria's Niger Delta, was lower than the average 21,900 barrels per day set in May, the company said. Cherwayko said analysts had expected output to be in about 30,000 barrels per day by now.
Abacan said its average production would be down because of "natural declines," workovers and the preparation of one previously producing well at the Ngo field for gas injection.
One uncertain factor in future production was whether the Ngo 6 exploration, currently being tested, would produce oil, he said.
Despite the postponed debt deal, Abacan does not face a cash crunch, he said.
"We just didn't feel comfortable taking the debt on without having questions answered, like is Ngo 6 going to produce or not," Cherwayko said. "It's just a prudent thing to do."
He said the company faced no problems with the producability of its oil reserves and expected to arrange some form of near-term financing for its development plans.
"We just decided to postpone debt now and just do another alternative type of financing in the interim and we could be back in the debt market in the near future."
Abacan stock in Toronto hit an all-time high of 15.50 on January 20. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
